docs.title: Day 1: Linux Fundamentals for Biologists
docs.text: Welcome to your first day of the IBDC-HPC Workshop. Today, we bridge the gap between biological data and computational power.

docs.title: 1. Why Linux for Biology? (30 mins)
docs.text:
Traditional operating systems often fail when handling large-scale genomic data.

  • Massive File Handling: Linux can read a 50GB FASTQ file in milliseconds, whereas Excel or Notepad would crash.
  • Stability: Linux systems are built to run for months, perfect for long-running bioinformatics pipelines.
  • Reproducibility: Every command you type can be saved in a script, ensuring your experiment can be repeated exactly by others.

docs.title: 2. Navigating the "Digital Lab" (The Map)
docs.text: Think of the Linux directory tree as your lab's storage room. Everything starts from the Root (/).

docs.title: Essential Navigation Commands
docs.text: Command Biology Context What it does pwd "Which shelf am I at?" Print Working Directory (shows your current path). ls -lh "Check the inventory." List files with human-readable sizes (MB/GB). cd "Walk to a new room." Change Directory (e.g., cd raw_data/). mkdir "Set up a new bench." Make Directory (e.g., mkdir mouse_project).

docs.title: 3. Managing Data Without a Mouse (The Action)
docs.text: In bioinformatics, we rarely click "Save As." Instead, we use commands to manipulate files.

docs.title: Viewing Data
docs.text:
• Peek at DNA reads: Don't open the whole file; just look at the top.
    • head -n 4 sample.fastq (Shows the first sequence read).
  • Check the end of a log:
    • tail -n 10 analysis.log (See if your process finished).

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
• Back up raw data: Always keep a copy before you start filtering.
    • cp raw_seq.fastq raw_seq_backup.fastq.
  • Organizing files:
    • mv results.txt ./final_output/ (Moves the file to the results folder).
  • Deleting (Warning!):
    • rm temp_file.txt (There is no recycle bin in Linux. It is gone forever!).

docs.title: 4. Practical Hands-on Exercise (60 mins)
docs.text:
Follow these steps in your terminal to create your first workspace.

  1. Create your folder: mkdir workshop_practice
  2. Enter the folder: cd workshop_practice
  3. Create a dummy sequence: echo "ATGCATGCATGC" > dna_sequence.txt
  4. Confirm the file exists: ls -l
  5. Check your current location: pwd (Ensure you see /home/harsha/workshop_practice).

docs.title: 5. Pro-Tips for Speed
docs.text:
• Tab Completion: Type the first 3 letters of a folder name and hit Tab. Linux will finish the word for you!.
  • Command History: Use the Up Arrow key to find commands you typed earlier.
  • Naming Rule: Never use spaces in filenames (e.g., use mouse_data.txt, not mouse data.txt).

docs.title: Purpose of This Workshop
docs.text: This workshop helps biologists become confident users of Linux and High-Performance Computing (HPC). The goal is to provide the practical understanding needed to manage, analyze, and interpret large datasets.

docs.title: Why Biologists Need Linux
docs.text: Modern research generates datasets (NGS, Multi-omics) that are: * Too large for personal computers. * Computationally intensive. * Requiring automation and reproducibility.

docs.title: 2. Introduction to Linux & Architecture
docs.text: Linux is a family of open-source operating systems based on a kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991.

docs.title: The Layered Structure
docs.text:
Linux architecture defines how components interact:

  1. Hardware Layer: Physical components like CPU, RAM, and HDD.
  2. Kernel: The "brain" that manages hardware resources and controls communication.
  3. System Libraries: Pre-written code that allows applications to interact with the kernel.
  4. The Shell: The command-line interpreter that serves as a bridge between the user and the kernel.
  5. User & Utilities: Tools for managing software, files, and users.

docs.title: 3. Linux File Hierarchy Structure (FHS)
docs.text: Everything in Linux starts from the Root (/). All files and directories appear under the root.

docs.title: Common Directories
docs.text:
• /bin: Important binary applications (tools).
  • /home: Residential zone where user data lives.
  • /tmp: Temporary storage; files here may be deleted upon reboot.
  • /etc: Control room containing configuration files.
  • /root: The home directory for the administrative root user.

docs.title: 4. The Linux Shell & Command Anatomy
docs.text: When you open the terminal, you are presented with a Prompt: username@hostname:~$.

docs.title: Command Syntax
docs.text:
The basic syntax is: command -options argument. Example: ls -l --sort time Documents/

  • Command: The "Verb" (what to do, e.g., ls).
  • Options/Switches: Change behavior (e.g., -l for long format).
  • Argument: The "Object" (what to act on, e.g., a folder).

Pro Tip: Spaces are critical. ls-l will fail; ls -l works.

docs.title: 5. Basic File and Folder Navigation
docs.text:
Use these commands to move through the "Digital Lab."

  • pwd: Print Working Directory (Where am I?).
  • ls -lhtr: List files in long format, human-readable, sorted by time (oldest first).
  • cd ..: Move up one level in the directory tree.
  • cd ~: Move back to your Home directory.
  • mkdir <dir>: Create a new directory.

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text:
• wc -l file1: Count the number of lines in a file.
  • head -n 100 file1: View the first 100 lines.
  • tail -n +2 file1: View from the 2nd line (perfect for skipping headers).
  • zcat file.gz | more: Peek into a compressed file page-by-page.

docs.title: Data Wrangling
docs.text:
• cut -f 1,4 file.tsv: Extract the 1st and 4th columns.
  • grep -w 'chr1' peaks.tsv: Search for the exact word 'chr1'.
  • awk '{print $3-$2}' file.bed: Subtract column 2 from column 3.
  • sort -V file1: Perform a version sort (ideal for chromosome names).

docs.title: 7. Meta Characters & Security
docs.text:
• Wildcards (*): Match multiple files (e.g., ls *.fastq).
  • Pipes (|): Join commands; output of one becomes input of the next.
  • Redirection (>): Save output to a file.
  • rm -rf <dir>: Danger Zone. Forcefully remove a directory and all its contents.

docs.title: 8. Reducing Fear and Anxiety
docs.text:
• Making mistakes is a normal part of learning.
  • You cannot damage the system through normal commands.
  • Users are not expected to memorize commands; use documentation as a reference.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Task Command Get Help man <command> or <command> --help Stop Process Ctrl + C Repeat Last !! Search History Ctrl + R

docs.title: Workshop Foundation: Linux & HPC for Biologists
Purpose of This Workshop
docs.text:
This workshop is designed to help biologists become confident users of Linux and High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments commonly used in modern biological research.

The goal is not to turn participants into system administrators or software developers, but to provide the practical understanding and confidence needed to work effectively on Linux systems and HPC platforms.

docs.title: What You Will Gain from This Workshop
docs.text:
By the end of this workshop, participants should be able to:

  • Understand what Linux and HPC systems are
  • Navigate files and directories on Linux systems
  • Follow and adapt command-line instructions
  • Run bioinformatics tools on servers or HPC
  • Submit, monitor, and manage jobs on IBDC-HPC
  • Use documentation to continue learning independently

docs.title: What This Workshop Is NOT
docs.text:
To reduce unnecessary stress, it is important to clarify that this workshop does not aim to teach:

  • Linux kernel development
  • Advanced system administration
  • Networking internals
  • Software engineering or programming concepts

These topics are outside the scope of this workshop.

docs.title: Why Biologists Need Linux and HPC
docs.text:
Modern biological research generates large and complex datasets, including:

  • Next-generation sequencing data
  • Mass spectrometry data
  • Imaging data
  • Multi-omics datasets

These datasets are often: - Too large for personal computers - Computationally intensive - Required to be processed in reproducible ways

Linux and HPC systems enable: - Efficient large-scale computation - Automation of analysis workflows - Reproducible and scalable research

docs.title: How Learning Will Happen in This Workshop
docs.text: This workshop follows a three-step learning approach:

docs.title: 1. Conceptual Understanding
docs.text: Participants first learn: - What the system does - Why certain tools and commands exist - How data and jobs move through the system

docs.title: 2. Guided Practical Sessions
docs.text: Participants then: - Follow step-by-step demonstrations - Type commands along with the instructor - Learn through small, controlled examples

docs.title: 3. Independent Revision and Practice
docs.text: After the workshop, participants can: - Revisit this documentation - Practice at their own pace - Apply concepts to their own research data

docs.title: A Simple Mental Model for Linux
docs.text:
Linux is not mysterious or complex when viewed correctly.

Think of Linux as a structured system that allows you to: - Store files - Organize data - Run programs - Automate repeated tasks

Key ideas: - Everything is organized into directories - Every file has a location - Commands are simple instructions to the system

docs.title: A Simple Mental Model for HPC
docs.text:
HPC systems can be understood using a simple analogy.

HPC is like a shared research facility: - Many users share powerful resources - You request resources instead of using them directly - Jobs wait in a queue - Results are produced later

Important concepts: - Login nodes are used for preparation - Compute nodes are used for execution - Job schedulers manage fairness and efficiency

docs.title: Reducing Fear and Anxiety
docs.text:
Participants should know that:

  • Making mistakes is a normal part of learning
  • Error messages provide useful information
  • Users cannot damage the system through normal commands
  • Asking questions is encouraged and welcomed

Learning Linux is a process, not a test.

docs.title: How to Use This Documentation
docs.text:
This documentation is intended to be:

  • A conceptual guide during the workshop
  • A reference for revision after the workshop
  • A support resource for future practice

Participants are not expected to memorize commands. Understanding concepts and workflows is the main objective.

docs.title: Workshop Ground Rules
docs.text:
• Type commands yourself during practice
  • Follow instructions step by step
  • Do not rush through exercises
  • Ask questions immediately if something is unclear
  • Support and help fellow participants

docs.title: What Success Looks Like
docs.text:
A participant has successfully completed the workshop if they can:

  • Log into a Linux or HPC system
  • Locate their data
  • Understand command-line instructions
  • Submit a computational job
  • Check job status and outputs
  • Know where to look for help

docs.title: Final Note
docs.text:
Linux and HPC are tools that empower biological research.

With the right foundation and guided practice, any biologist can learn to use them effectively.
